name: Hanako-san
description: Hanako-san is a Japanese school ghost said to inhabit the third stall of the third-floor girls' bathroom and to answer when summoned with a specific knocking ritual. She is one of the most widely circulated school-based urban legends in modern Japan.
full_description: Hanako-san (花子さん, 'Miss Hanako'), commonly called Toire no Hanako-san ('Hanako of the Toilet'), is a Japanese yokai/yurei tied to school bathrooms. She is described as the spirit of a young girl with a bobbed haircut and a red skirt or dress who haunts a particular stall — usually the third stall of the third-floor girls' restroom — and can be summoned by knocking three times on the door and asking 'Are you there, Hanako-san?' If she answers, consequences in different versions range from a bloody hand pulling the questioner into the toilet, to being dragged to Hell, to encountering a three-headed lizard. Folklorists trace the schoolyard legend to roughly the 1950s; it became a national cultural fixture during the Japanese kokkuri/yokai boom of the late 1980s and the school-horror media wave of the 1990s. There is no canonical origin story: variants attribute her death to a WWII air raid during a game of hide-and-seek, to murder by a parent or stranger, or to bullying-driven suicide. The legend is closely associated with children's storytelling games and 'school seven mysteries' (gakkō no nana fushigi) traditions.
origin: Japan-wide schoolyard urban legend, with regional variants in nearly every prefecture. The legend has been exported through anime, manga, films, and the global creepypasta and J-horror communities.

etymology.origin: Japanese post-war schoolyard urban legend; the name 'Hanako' is a generic, common Japanese girl's name often used in folklore and exemplar contexts (analogous to English 'Jane Doe').
etymology.meaning: 'Hanako' (花子) literally 'flower child'; 'Toire no Hanako-san' translates as 'Hanako of the Toilet'.
etymology.first_use: Documented in Japanese schoolyard folklore by the 1950s; widely popularized nationally in the late 1980s.

timeline.event: Earliest stratum of the Hanako-san schoolyard legend, per folklorist Matthew Meyer
timeline.significance: Establishes the legend as a postwar phenomenon

timeline.event: Hanako-san spreads broadly through schoolyards as part of the late-1980s yokai/kokkuri-san boom
timeline.significance: Transition from local oral tradition to nationally recognized children's legend
timeline.source: Foster, Michael Dylan, The Book of Yokai (2015)

timeline.event: Live-action film Toire no Hanako-san directed by Joji Matsuoka released in Japan
timeline.significance: First major mainstream cinematic treatment; portrayed Hanako sympathetically

timeline.event: Shinsei Toire no Hanako-san directed by Yukihiko Tsutsumi released, depicting a vengeful Hanako
timeline.significance: Cemented Hanako-san as a horror genre icon

timeline.event: AidaIro begins serialization of Jibaku Shōnen Hanako-kun ('Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun')
timeline.significance: Reframes the legend with a male protagonist and launches a major modern franchise

timeline.event: Anime adaptation of Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun by studio Lerche premieres
timeline.significance: Brings the legend to a global audience through streaming platforms

cultural_notes: Predominantly treated as a children's game-legend rather than a sincere ghost belief; nonetheless, Hanako-san is widely recognized across Japan as a stock supernatural figure of the school setting.

sources.title: The Book of Yokai: Mysterious Creatures of Japanese Folklore
